summary: A builder page. Its file also draws the document skeleton every view sits in, once.

root.note: The whole document: head, then body.

elements.note: Only what the contract owns, which a page fixture compares (SC-019): the link to the served salt.css, then the scriptless phone layout's noscript. Each platform writes the rest of head natively, and the comparison ignores it (normalise.mjs pageOf).

href.value: from:the address the platform serves styles/salt.css at
href.note: Its file name is salt.css, which is how the comparison finds it among the platform's own links; the address itself is the platform's, and the conformance runner's stylesheet pin compares the bytes served there.

children.note: The one shared stylesheet bundle, served verbatim (SC-002, SC-018).

children.when: consent is pending and the site's consent condition holds (the consent ruling below): an integration needs consent and, on WordPress, a WP Consent API plugin is wired

headings.note: The first heading-providing section claims the h1; otherwise fallback-heading draws it.

notes.text: The scriptless style in the head is the one inline style element the contract draws, and nothing it draws carries a style attribute (section#no-inline-style, SC-029). A target with a strict Content-Security-Policy (no 'unsafe-inline' for styles) allows that element by a hash or a nonce, and keeps its contents byte for byte as written here, so a hash of them stays valid; Salt for WordPress allows it by the sha256 of its exact contents.

The consent banner and the footer's consent control are drawn on one condition (SC-006, SC-030; proposed, for founder approval at contract review): the site runs an integration that needs consent, which is a consent category in use (a fixture's site.consent.categories is not empty), and on Salt for WordPress a WP Consent API plugin is also wired (wp_has_consent exists). Without one, WordPress keeps every integration that needs consent denied, failing closed as salt_consent() does, and draws neither. Salt for Next.js's own consent store is always wired, so its condition is the integration alone. A wired mechanism with no category in use draws neither: a visitor has nothing to choose. Salt for WordPress ports Salt for Next.js's banner, gate, preferences panel, categories and cookie format; a client that needs a certified consent tool (Google Ads personalisation in the UK and EEA) uses one as a Grain override.

The scriptless phone layout is the noscript style in head: with no script it keeps the header's menu and call to action on screen below the breakpoint, hides the burger nothing could open, and lets the row wrap, through the three custom properties chrome.css reads. It sits in head because a style element inside noscript is conforming only there; a no-js class removed by script was rejected because it needs a blocking script and leaves a phone whose script fails mid-page with no menu.

A page fixture compares the body and the head elements above (SC-019): the comparison drops the head's other content, the html and body elements' attributes, and the script, style and link elements in the body, which are each platform's delivery (the contract's body markup draws none of them), and reads the stylesheet's href as its file name.

owes: Rename skip-link to salt-skip-link; chrome.css draws it hidden until focused.
The header's noscript style in the document head, moved from inside the header.

salt-skip-link; tabindex -1 on main; the hidden h1 as fallback-heading; the consent banner, gate, preferences panel, categories and cookie format ported from Salt for Next.js, drawn only when the consent condition holds: an integration needs consent and a WP Consent API plugin is wired; without one every such integration stays denied (SC-006, SC-030).
